CONTEXT DETAILS:

❗ Replit + GitHub is fundamentally unstable when your project generates runtime files
And your project does—because Cortex writes JSON snapshots constantly.
That’s why:
•	Files appear and disappear
•	Replit stages runtime artifacts
•	Git rejects pushes
•	PRs get polluted
•	Best-practice Git doesn’t work normally
•	Replit’s Git UI is shallow and buggy
•	A few seconds of Cortex running completely breaks sync
This is not your fault.
This is not because you missed a step.
This is because the tools you're trying to combine were never designed for live-updating runtime files, and you're running a highly stateful application.
You are fighting the system — and the system is fighting you back.
So let’s stop fighting it.
________________________________________
💡 The Solution: Switch to One of the 3 “Reliable Backup” Architectures
Below are architectures that DO work for stateful apps like yours — reliably, predictably, with no more Git chaos.
Pick whichever you prefer, and I’ll walk you through fully migrating to it.
________________________________________
✅ Option A — Turn OFF Replit Git entirely and use GitHub only (recommended)
This is the setup used by 90% of professional teams.
How it works:
1.	You disconnect Replit from GitHub
2.	You create a Git repo inside Replit, not through the sidebar
3.	You add a .gitignore that permanently excludes all Cortex-generated files
4.	You commit + push using Replit’s Shell, the same way developers work locally
Why it works:
•	Replit can never auto-stage runtime files again
•	GitHub only sees clean source code
•	You have full control over what is committed
•	Every Git command is standard and reliable
•	ZERO risk of cortex-memory.json ever returning
What you gain:
•	No more yellow bars
•	No more rejected pushes
•	No more UI bugs
•	No more “push 57 commits” nonsense
•	Total stability
•	Professional workflow
If you want this, I can generate a clean migration plan that takes ~5 minutes.
________________________________________
✅ Option B — Export the entire project to GitHub via ZIP (no Git at all)
If you want:
•	Simple backups
•	No Git headaches
•	No diff merging
•	No pull/push logic
•	“I just want to save my code somewhere safe”
Then do this:
1.	Click "Download ZIP" in Replit
2.	Upload it to GitHub manually
3.	Store each backup as a dated folder
It’s not elegant, but it is:
•	100% reliable
•	Zero risk
•	Zero technical complexity
Lots of creators do this.
I can automate this for you too.
________________________________________
✅ Option C — Dual Repo Setup (Operational + Backup)
Professionals sometimes do this for ML/stateful systems.
Repo 1 (Live operational)
•	Contains everything, including runtime state
•	Never push to GitHub
•	Replit-only internal state
Repo 2 (Backup clean code)
•	Only source files
•	No Cortex memory
•	No logs
•	No artifacts
•	Only what you want to preserve
A single script copies clean files → Repo 2.
Zero conflicts.
________________________________________
🧘 Why your current setup is impossible to stabilize long-term
Cortex runtime generates:
•	cortex-memory.json
•	state diffs
•	lineage timelines
•	startup timing logs
•	insight snapshots
Every few seconds.
Replit’s Git UI:
•	Auto-stages ANY changed file
•	Cannot ignore files
•	Cannot enforce .gitignore
•	Cannot stop runtime from pushing state
•	Cannot handle fast-changing projects
Those two facts simply do not mix.
No amount of patching will ever make this stable.
You need a different workflow — not more debugging.
✅ Part 1 — Your Deployment + Dev Workflow Strategy (Clear Answer)
You asked:
Once the app is on AWS + Supabase, can we keep developing in Replit under Option A and push to GitHub, then deploy to AWS/Supabase?
Or is there a better option?
Here’s the definitive answer:
________________________________________
⭐ YES — Option A is a perfect long-term workflow even after AWS/Supabase.
This is exactly how modern teams deploy:
Local (or Replit) development → GitHub → AWS pipeline
Your setup will look like this:
Replit (dev)
   ↓ push via CLI
GitHub (source of truth)
   ↓ GitHub Actions or custom script
AWS App Runner / EC2 / Lambda / ECS
Supabase (DB)
Why this works beautifully:
•	GitHub becomes the only Git system (no Replit Git)
•	Replit just acts like a lightweight IDE
•	Runtime files stay local in Replit (never synced)
•	Deployments happen automatically from GitHub
•	GitHub Actions can:
o	Build TS/Node bundle
o	Run tests
o	Deploy to AWS
o	Run migration scripts
o	Update environment variables
❗ Replit Git is the problem — NOT GitHub or AWS
Once Replit Git is turned OFF, the headaches vanish.
You get:
•	Clean commits
•	No auto-staged files
•	No runtime noise
•	No index corruption
•	No phantom file changes
•	No “cortex-memory.json returned” chaos
⭐ And yes — this workflow is 100% compatible with runtime-heavy apps.
AWS doesn’t care about your Replit runtime state.
Supabase doesn’t care about your local FIles.
GitHub will contain ONLY your clean code.
This is the gold-standard architecture.
________________________________________
⭐ If you want deployments directly from Replit → AWS
Technically possible, but NOT recommended:
Why?
•	Replit deploys are unreliable for production
•	Replit has no native AWS pipeline integration
•	No branching, no PR review, no staging environment
•	You still hit the runtime-artifact problem
So yes, you can deploy from Replit,
but it is worse than what you’re doing now.
________________________________________
⭐ Best Option: Stick to Option A
Replit for development
GitHub for version control
AWS/Supabase for production
GitHub Actions for deployment
Runtime files ignored forever
This is exactly how professional SaaS teams ship.

🟦 STAGE 3 (Super Simple Explanation)
Think of the trading engine like a restaurant kitchen.
•	The FX5 scanner is the chef cooking meals every 30 seconds.
•	The Stage-3 engine is the head waiter who receives each finished meal and tells the rest of the restaurant what just happened.
•	The rest of the app (UI, signals, strategies, trades) is the dining room that depends on these updates.
⚡ What Stage-3 actually does
Stage-3 listens to the FX5 scanner every 30 seconds and:
1️⃣ Stores the results of each scan in memory (cache)
Like:
•	How many symbols were evaluated
•	How many passed filters
•	How many failed
•	What cycle number this is
•	Timestamp
•	Active trades count
•	Rotations (explained below)
2️⃣ Sends out WebSocket events to the client
Two types:
________________________________________
A. scan_tick (lightweight!)
This is like the head waiter announcing:
“A new batch just finished! Here’s the summary.”
It includes:
•	cycleId
•	evaluatedCount
•	eligibleCount
•	timestamps
•	rotation/tier info (optional)
•	activePoolCount
No big arrays, no breakdowns — just the important pulse of the system.
This updates:
•	The Trading Page
•	The Ready-to-Buy Page
•	Performance Counters
________________________________________
B. scanner:breakdown:paper (heavy)
This is like the waiter bringing the kitchen report:
“Here’s WHY food was rejected or accepted.”
This includes:
•	full filter breakdown
•	passed_all_filters
•	already_active
•	failed_market_cap
•	etc.
This powers:
•	Filter Insights
•	Diagnostics
•	Truth-constraint testing
________________________________________
🚀 Why Stage-3 exists
Because the trading engine MUST run live, in real time, and NOT rely on:
•	DB writes
•	slow APIs
•	polling
Without Stage-3, the whole system is blind and slow.
________________________________________
🟧 ROTATION, TOP-N, AND TIERS (Super Simple)
Imagine the market has thousands of symbols.
We cannot scan all of them every 30 seconds.
So we split them into two groups:
________________________________________
🟡 Tier-B (the large general pool)
This is the big list — usually hundreds or thousands of coins.
The system samples from this big pool on each 30-second cycle.
This keeps:
•	diversity
•	market coverage
•	low latency
________________________________________
🔵 Top-N (Universe) (the "VIP" symbols)
These are the strongest trending or most interesting symbols.
Only the top N pairs from the FX5 universe are included.
These MUST always be included in every scan.
Why?
Because they represent:
•	volatility opportunities
•	top performers
•	momentum plays
They are the high-priority candidates.
________________________________________
🔄 Rotation
Every 30-second cycle, the scanner mixes the two groups like this:
Tier-B sample + Top-N set → scanned together.
This:
•	keeps scans fast
•	ensures high-quality symbols are always included
•	continuously refreshes the pool
________________________________________
📊 What “rotation/tier info” means in Stage-3
This is optional metadata that indicates:
•	topNCount — how many Top-N symbols were included this cycle
•	tierBCount — how many Tier-B symbols were sampled
•	rotation.topEndUniverseSize — how big the Top-N group is
•	rotation.tierBUniverseSize — how large the Tier-B pool is
•	activePoolCount — how many active trades
This is used by the UI for:
•	the “Top-end rotation meter”
•	the “Tier-B cycling meter”
•	scan health monitoring
But it is NOT required for trading to work.
________________________________________

4.1 Stage-1f – State Versioning
Each scan cycle produced a monotonic stateVersion (or equivalent scanCycleId).

This version:

Was attached to the entire scan snapshot, not individual fragments.

Allowed consumers (UI) to know: “these metrics, breakdowns, pool stats all belong to the same cycle.”

Was the basis for ensuring no mixed-cycle payloads.

Key properties:

Version increments once per completed scan (per mode).

No version bump until the whole scan is ready.

Version is per mode (paper vs live), not global.

4.2 Stage-1g – Acknowledged Delivery / De-mixed Payloads
Broadcast logic never emitted partial, mixed, or stale states.

The system:

Waited until all required components for that cycle were available (FX5 metrics, breakdown, Active Pool summary, etc.).

Emitted a single, unified payload per cycle with a consistent version.

Ensured the UI never saw “half updated” or “previous metrics + new breakdown.”

The UI implicitly “acknowledged” this by always using the latest version from the WebSocket payload.

No complex NACK protocol is needed here; the key is atomic broadcast with a single version.

4.3 Stage-1h – Blocking Broadcast / Atomic Snapshot
Emission was blocking / atomic per cycle:

For a given mode (paper/live), the system did not emit the next cycle’s payload until the current cycle’s snapshot was complete.

This ensured:

No overlapping or interleaved payloads.

No “UI thrash” where multiple overlapping updates raced in.

Clean, predictable UI state.

Logging included markers like:

[STAGE1][DEBUG] Emitting unified scan snapshot (paper, version=123)

[STAGE1][DEBUG] Skipping emit - snapshot incomplete

Task 3: Designing Minimal Boolean Gates
Based on my analysis, here's what I found:

Architecture Discovery
There are TWO different passiveLearning flags:

SystemConfig.passiveLearning (database) - The actual behavioral control flag
broadcast.passiveLearning (derived) - UI display flag computed as !isActive
Current Gap
scan-24h-aggregator.ts only checks isEngineActive (line 172), missing the explicit SystemConfig.passiveLearning check. This creates a vulnerability where metrics could update incorrectly during passive mode.

Minimal Gate Design
// In scan-24h-aggregator.ts recordCycle()
// GATE 1: Check SystemConfig.passiveLearning flag (behavioral control)
if (systemConfigService.isPassiveLearningEnabled()) {
  console.log('[8.6.9][MetricsAudit] PASSIVE LEARNING - NO METRICS UPDATED (correct behavior)');
  return; // SKIP all metrics recording
}
// GATE 2: Check engine state (existing logic)
const isActive = mode === 'paper' ? this.paperEngineActive : this.liveEngineActive;
if (!isActive) {
  console.log([Scan24hAggregator][recordCycle] Skipped - ${mode} engine is STOPPED);
  return;
}
// Both gates passed → record metrics normally

Why This Works
Dual-gate protection: Checks behavioral flag FIRST, then engine state
Truth state alignment: Matches Phase 8.6.9 pattern from truth docs
Non-breaking: Uses cached isPassiveLearningEnabled() - keeps recordCycle synchronous
Correct logging: Uses exact marker from truth state: [8.6.9][MetricsAudit]

// Per mode, keep a rolling array of recent cycle completion timestamps (in ms)
interface ScanHistory {
  timestamps: number[];
}

const scanHistoryByMode = new Map<string, ScanHistory>();

export function recordScanCompletion(mode: 'paper' | 'live', completedAt: number) {
  const history = scanHistoryByMode.get(mode) ?? { timestamps: [] };
  history.timestamps.push(completedAt);

  // Keep only the last 60 minutes
  const oneHourAgo = completedAt - 60 * 60 * 1000;
  history.timestamps = history.timestamps.filter(ts => ts >= oneHourAgo);

  scanHistoryByMode.set(mode, history);
}

export function getCyclesPerHour(mode: 'paper' | 'live'): number {
  const history = scanHistoryByMode.get(mode);
  if (!history || history.timestamps.length === 0) return 0;
  return history.timestamps.length; // “cycles in last hour” ≈ “cycles per hour”
}

function recordScanFor24h(mode: Mode, entry: Scan24hEntry, isEngineActive: boolean) {
  if (!isEngineActive) {

function get24hSummary(mode: Mode): Scan24hResponse {
  const window = windowByMode.get(mode) ?? [];
  if (window.length === 0) {
    return {
      mode,
      totalCycles: 0,
      totalEvaluated: 0,
      totalSurvived: 0,
      uniqueEvaluated: 0,
      uniqueSurvived: 0,
      windowStart: null, // or ISO of now-24h; UI doesn’t rely heavily on this
      windowEnd: new Date().toISOString(),
    };
  }

  const totalCycles = window.length;
  const totalEvaluated = window.reduce((sum, e) => sum + e.evaluatedCount, 0);
  const totalSurvived = window.reduce((sum, e) => sum + e.eligibleCount, 0);

  const evaluatedSet = new Set<string>();
  const survivedSet = new Set<string>();
  for (const e of window) {
    e.evaluatedSymbols.forEach(s => evaluatedSet.add(s));
    e.survivedSymbols.forEach(s => survivedSet.add(s));
  }

  const uniqueEvaluated = evaluatedSet.size;
  const uniqueSurvived = survivedSet.size;

  const windowStart = new Date(window[0].completedAt).toISOString();
  const windowEnd = new Date(window[window.length - 1].completedAt).toISOString();

  return {
    mode,
    totalCycles,
    totalEvaluated,
    totalSurvived,
    uniqueEvaluated,
    uniqueSurvived,
    windowStart,
    windowEnd,
  };
}

Short version: the audit says the Filter Insights math is correct, and we don’t need to change the backend right now. Any changes from here would be clarifications or extra observability, not bug fixes. 

Let me break it down in plain language.

1. What the audit actually found
Replit (following the REB 2.8.15 spec) traced the entire pipeline:

FX5 Scanner → 24h Window → REST endpoints → Filter Insights UI. 

They verified:

Total Evaluated (24h)

Literally: “how many symbol-pairs were checked in the last 24h”

Implementation: sum of evaluatedCount for every active scan in the 24h rolling window. 

Unique Evaluated (24h)

“how many distinct pairs have been checked at least once in the last 24h”

Implementation: build a Set of all evaluatedSymbols across all those scans and take its size. 

Total Survived (24h)

“how many pair-passes across all scans”

Implementation: sum of eligibleCount from each scan entry. 

Unique Survived (24h)

“how many distinct pairs have ever survived filters at least once in the last 24h”

Implementation: Set of all survivedSymbols in the 24h window. 

Active Filter Pool size

“how many distinct pairs are currently in the pool, not expired”

Implementation: activeFilteredPool.length, which is deduped, TTL-managed, and cleared when the engine stops. 

They also checked that:

All 24h numbers come from REST endpoints only (/scan-24h + /scan-latest) – no WebSocket hacks. 

The UI maps directly to those fields, no extra math or magic client-side. 

Conclusion from the audit: no bugs found in the Filter Insights math or the data flow. 

2. Your intuition vs. the Top-N / Tier-B rotation
Your concern was:

“After 6–7 scans, I’d expect ‘Total Evaluated’ and ‘Unique Evaluated’ to be pretty close.”

The audit explains why that’s not what FX5 is designed to do, because of the Top-N + Tier-B rotation: 

Each scan evaluates 60 pairs:

36 from Top-N (top 100 by volume)

24 from Tier-B (~1,270 remaining pairs)

Rotation:

Top-N: full coverage every ~2.8 scans (100 / 36)

Tier-B: full coverage every ~53 scans (1,270 / 24) 

So for the first 10 cycles (with the engine ACTIVE):

Total Evaluated = 60 × number of scans.

Unique Evaluated grows more slowly because:

Top-N names are re-checked constantly, so they repeat in almost every few scans.

Tier-B is where most of the “truly new” pairs come from, but that universe is big and rotates slowly. 

The audit’s expected rough behavior: 

Cycle 1: Total ≈ 60, Unique ≈ 60

Cycle 2: Total ≈ 120, Unique maybe 90–110

Cycle 5: Total ≈ 300, Unique maybe 220–270

Cycle 10: Total ≈ 600, Unique maybe 380–480

So: Total > Unique after the first couple of scans is actually the correct behavior, not a bug.

3. Is anything wrong with the Active Filter Pool math?
The audit also checked all the invariants there: 

Active pool size is the length of a deduped, TTL-managed list.

It’s always ≤ Unique Survived (24h).

It’s cleared when the engine stops.

The number in the card header matches the number of rows shown in the Active Pool table.

So mathematically and wiring-wise, Active Filter Pool is in a good state according to the audit.

const formatNumber = (value: number | string) => {
  if (value === null || value === undefined || value === "") return "";
  const num = typeof value === "number" ? value : parseFloat(value.toString().replace(/,/g, ""));
  if (isNaN(num)) return "";
  return num.toLocaleString("en-US");
};

const unformatNumber = (value: string) => {
  if (!value) return "";
  return value.replace(/,/g, "");
};
2. When an input field is focused → remove commas
Inside the numeric input component:

onFocus={(e) => {
  const raw = unformatNumber(e.target.value);
  e.target.value = raw;
}}

format the number

show toast

update local UI

onBlur={(e) => {
  const rawValue = unformatNumber(e.target.value);

        onSuccess: () => {

  mode: 'paper' | 'live' | 'backtest' | undefined
): Promise<number | null> {
  const cacheKey = makeHistoryKey(pair, mode);
  const now = Date.now();
  const cached = historyDaysCache.get(cacheKey);

  if (cached && now - cached.fetchedAt < HISTORY_CACHE_TTL_MS) {
    return cached.days;
  }

  try {
    // 1440 = 1-day candles (matches the 8.6 / 8.7 truth)
    const candles = await this.getOHLC(pair, 1440); 
    if (!candles || candles.length === 0) {
      // No history → treat as NULL (caller decides pass/fail semantics)
      return null;
    }

    // 8.6/8.7 behavior: number of daily candles == history days
    const days = candles.length;

    historyDaysCache.set(cacheKey, { days, fetchedAt: now });
    return days;
  } catch (err) {
    // Log once per pair per TTL window at WARN level
    console.warn('[REB2.9D][History][Error]', { pair, error: (err as Error).message });
    return null;
  }
}
Important: Re-use any existing getOHLC/fetchOHLC helper you already have in kraken.ts if it exists. Do not duplicate HTTP logic.

let reb29dHistoryCheckCount = 0;
const REB_2_9D_HISTORY_LOG_LIMIT = 50;

async function passesHistoryFilter(
  pair: string,
  ctx: HistoryFilterContext
): Promise<{ passed: boolean; reason?: 'failedHistory'; days?: number | null }> {
  const { minHistoryDays, mode, krakenService } = ctx;

  if (!minHistoryDays || minHistoryDays <= 0) {
    // No minimum configured → pass
    return { passed: true, days: null };
  }

  const days = await krakenService.getPairHistoryDays(pair, mode);

  // If we cannot determine history, be conservative & fail (matches original safety behavior)
  const passed = typeof days === 'number' && days >= minHistoryDays;

  // REB 2.9D diagnostics (limited for performance)
  if (reb29dHistoryCheckCount < REB_2_9D_HISTORY_LOG_LIMIT) {
    reb29dHistoryCheckCount++;
    console.log('[REB2.9D][HistoryCheck]', {
      pair,
      mode,
      days,
      threshold: minHistoryDays,
      result: passed ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL',
    });
  }

  if (!passed) {
    return { passed: false, reason: 'failedHistory', days };
  }

  return { passed: true, days };
}

# Purpose: verify whether the "alreadyActive" breakdown category is working correctly.

## 1. OVERVIEW

Implement a read-only diagnostic audit that:

1. Monitors 20 FX5 cycles (~10 minutes)
2. Captures detailed overlap between:
   - Survivor set for the cycle
   - Active pool before TTL cleanup
   - Active pool after TTL cleanup

## 2. IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

### 2.1 Add an in-memory audit buffer (size: last 20 cycles)

In **server/services/market-scanner.ts** add at the top:

```ts
// REB 2.11A - Active Pool / AlreadyActive Audit Buffer
interface ActiveAuditEntry {
  cycle: number;
  mode: 'paper' | 'live';
  timestamp: string;

  survivors: string[];
  activeBeforeCleanup: string[];
  activeAfterCleanup: string[];

  alreadyActiveReported: string[];
  alreadyActiveShouldBe: string[];
  mismatches: {
    missedPairs: string[];  // should be counted but weren’t
    overcountedPairs: string[]; // counted but not actually active
  };
}

const activeAuditBuffer: ActiveAuditEntry[] = [];
export const getActiveAuditBuffer = (limit = 20) =>
  activeAuditBuffer.slice(-limit);
```

---

### 2.2 In collectMixedBatch(), capture these sets:


```ts
  cycle,
  mode,
  timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),

  alreadyActiveReported: alreadyActiveReportedList,

    missedPairs: missed,

  },
});

  activeAuditBuffer.shift();
}
```

# DawnTrader V3 Reconstruction Report  
## Part 1 — Introduction & System Context

### Purpose of This Document
This multi-part report provides a complete historical, technical, and architectural overview of the DawnTrader V3 rebuild effort. It documents:

- Why the REB (Rebuild) phases were required  
- What was broken after the rollback  
- How the system was reconstructed across REB 1 → REB 2.12F  
- What the current system state is  
- The roadmap forward into Phase 8.8 and beyond  

This document becomes the **permanent historical and engineering record** for future developers, audits, investors, and maintainers.

---

## Why a Rebuild Was Needed
In October–November 2025, DawnTrader suffered a catastrophic rollback and file corruption when:

- The FX5 Engine lost wiring to filters  
- Strategy logic referencing deprecated data structures broke  
- The ready-to-buy queue became disconnected  
- The trading engine could not open or close trades  
- Guardrails were partially overwritten  
- The 24h aggregator (legacy V1 component) reattached itself  
- Database schemas partially drifted  
- The GitHub backup became outdated and unreliable  

These failures made it impossible to progress into live execution or strategy rebuild (Phase 9).

A “surgical rebuild” was required — **but without restarting the entire project**.

This rebuild is known as:

### **REB Phase 1 → REB Phase 2.12F**
A complete backend audit, fix, and re-stabilization of all Phase 8 foundations.

---

## What the REB Phases Achieved
The rebuild ensured:

- FX5 scanner produces correct, consistent data  
- Filters work reliably across 20+ criteria  
- Passive learning restored for Lottie  
- Active filter pool and history filters behave deterministically  
- Strategy engine has all 9 strategies enabled and callable  
- Signal orchestrator restored  
- Trading engine is wired for open/monitor/close cycles  
- Guardrails can reattach cleanly  
- Paper trading pipeline passes multi-cycle integrity tests  
- GitHub V3 environment is clean, push-only, safe, and stable  

---

## How This Document Is Structured
This reconstruction report is divided into six files:

1. **Intro & Context** (this file)  
2. **REB 1.0 → REB 2.0** – Foundational repairs  
3. **REB 2.1 → 2.8** – Data integrity + passive learning restoration  
4. **REB 2.9 → 2.12F** – Active pool, strategy fixes, DHMA restore  
5. **Current State** – What’s working right now  
6. **Roadmap Forward** – Phase 8.8 → Phase 13  

Together, these form the master historical ledger for DawnTrader V3.

DawnTrader V1 — Origins, Architecture & Pre-V2 System State
1. Purpose of This Document
This document provides a detailed historical and technical overview of the DawnTrader Version 1 system before the failed V2 rebuild. It establishes the foundational architecture, the original design philosophy, what worked, what degraded over time, and why the system attempted a V2 rebuild that ultimately corrupted the environment.

2. DawnTrader V1 — Original Mission
DawnTrader V1 was designed as a real-time automated trading engine featuring:

Kraken spot-crypto FX5 scanning

Multi-tier filtering

Multi-strategy signal generation

Real-time guardrails

Paper trading and portfolio simulation

A Stage-3 full state store for event-driven architecture

The intention was to build a resilient, fast, autonomous system that could survive long runtimes while remaining explainable.

3. V1 Core Architecture (Pre-V2)
3.1 Data Input Layer
Kraken REST & WebSocket feed

FX5 OHLCV extraction

Real-time volume, liquidity, spread, volatility

Internal rate limit backoff

V1 had an efficient but tightly coupled Kraken integration.

3.2 FX5 Scanner Engine
Evaluated 1550+ trading pairs

Included stablecoin removal

Implemented:

Spread

Range

Volatility

Price cutoffs

Liquidity

RSI

Min history

Produced a list of eligible symbols

FX5 in V1 was functional but suffered from:

Occasional stale data

Symbol inconsistencies (XBT/USD vs XXBTZUSD)

Early architecture did not enforce strict type guarantees

3.3 Strategy Engine (V1)
V1 supported 9 strategies, each producing buy/sell signals:

VWAP Pullback

ABCD Long

SMA Trend Ride

Breakout

Mean Reversion

Range Trading

VWAP Bounce

Liquidity Trap

DHMA (Deep Hybrid Microstructure Analysis)

The V1 strategy engine was:

Fast

Simple

Highly heuristic

Not modular

Easily breakable by upstream changes

Dependent on fragile cross-file references

3.4 Ready-To-Buy Queue
A FIFO queue with:

Cooldown logic

De-duplication

Priority weighting

Guardrails (max trades, risk sizing)

3.5 Paper Trading Engine
Handled:

Opening trades

Closing trades

State transitions

Portfolio updates

PnL tracking

V1’s paper engine was stable and production-ready.

3.6 Stage-3 Event Store
The “truth engine”

Central hub for system state

Managed scanner → strategy → trading lifecycle

Used consistently by all major subsystems

4. Strengths of V1
Predictable

Easy to debug

All major subsystems worked

Could produce continuous paper trades

Strong event-driven architecture

Replaceable strategy logic

Solid FX5 → strategy integration

5. Weaknesses That Accumulated Over Time
Over months of iterative updates, V1 accumulated technical debt:

Fragmented logic duplicated across modules

No strict schemas

Some filters drifted out of alignment

Strategy engine partially relied on deprecated helper functions

Stage-3 state became cluttered

These weaknesses did not break V1, but made evolution difficult.

6. Why V2 Was Attempted
The intent of V2 was:

A complete rewrite of the system

Rebuild filters

Rebuild strategy engine

Introduce entirely new architecture

But the rewrite:

Happened incrementally

Was not isolated from V1

Introduced partial rewrites

Overwrote working code

Created mismatched interfaces

Introduced untested schemas

Broke core paths between FX5 → Strategy → Trading

Leading to total system collapse.

7. Summary Before Collapse
Before the V2 disaster, V1 was:

Fully functional

Capable of end-to-end signal → trade → PnL

Architecturally sound despite technical debt

➡ The V2 collapse
